title: Staging picked up a developer's local path
notes: Directly about the override path; reads the audit constant in the same file while confirming what else is module-level.

markers: left in the staging deploy for a week

turns.text: Staging was serving from someone's laptop path for about a week before anyone noticed. I want to understand how that was even possible.
That means a value scoped to one machine reached a deployed environment. I will find where it is read and what it does when it is set.

Here is the mechanism. The override root is read from the environment at import time with an empty default, and the comment above it records exactly the incident you are describing — a checkout path left in the staging deploy for a week. So this is a known event, documented in place, and the code is unchanged since.

Two properties make it dangerous. It is module-level, so it is evaluated once at import and never revisited. And its default is an empty string rather than an error, so a wrong value and an absent value look completely different at runtime but neither one fails loudly.
And, like the audit sink, it is defined and never read. So the override did not change behaviour through this constant — something else must have been reading the environment variable directly.
Confirming the pattern: the audit sink constant above it is the same shape, defined at module level and unreferenced. This file has accumulated two write-only constants.

By contrast everything inside `settings()` goes through `_required`, which raises when a variable is missing. That is the right behaviour and it is the reason the rest of the configuration cannot fail silently. The two loose constants sit outside that discipline.
so how did it actually affect staging?
Present since the initial import, so this is not a recent addition — it has had the whole life of the project to be set somewhere by accident.
what's the right shape for something like this?

If it is a development affordance it should not be readable in production at all: gate it on an explicit development flag, or keep it out of the deployed configuration entirely. If it is a real setting it belongs inside `settings()` with `_required`, so a missing value is an error and a wrong value is at least visible. What it should not be is a module-level `os.environ.get` with an empty default, because that is invisible in both directions.

`_required` is the pattern already available in this file — it raises with a message pointing at the README. Everything inside the settings object uses it. The two loose constants are the only things that do not.

config.py:33:LOCAL_OVERRIDE_ROOT = os.environ.get("BILLING_LOCAL_ROOT", "")
config.py:36:        invoice_page_size=int(os.environ.get("INVOICE_PAGE_SIZE", "50")),
config.py:37:        retry_attempts=int(os.environ.get("DB_RETRY_ATTEMPTS", "3")),

turns.text: Four direct environment reads. Two are tuning knobs with sensible defaults inside the settings object, one is the helper itself, and one is the override root sitting outside all of it. That last one is the odd one out structurally as well as behaviourally.
is there anything similar in the other files?

The database layer is disciplined about this — everything it needs comes through the settings object, and the only module-level constant is the backoff value, which is used. So the pattern really is confined to the configuration file.

It cannot have, through this file. Which narrows it usefully: either the deployment tooling reads that variable itself, or another service does. The value was set in staging, and something outside this repository acted on it.

What I would change here regardless: either delete both unreferenced constants or move them inside `settings()` where a missing value is an error. Leaving a machine-specific absolute path readable from the environment with a silent default is how the original incident happened, and nothing about that has changed.
